domain: designing, running, evaluating, and governing one-prompt multi-agent improvement loops
refresh_cadence: monthly for model and harness behavior; quarterly for research literature; before every integration or release for platform controls, pricing, and limits

confidence_policy.evidence-based: Controlled research or authoritative primary data, scoped to the population and tasks actually studied.
confidence_policy.practitioner: First-party field report, vendor engineering guidance, repository evidence, or operational judgment. Useful, but not a controlled causal result.
confidence_policy.contested: Mixed, contradicted, stale, or otherwise insufficient evidence. It must be presented with its caveat.
confidence_policy.folklore: Popular claim without credible support. It is recorded only to prevent accidental promotion to fact.

researched_requires: at least two captured sources for fast-moving or high-stakes domains
at least one official or primary source for lower-risk domains
retrieved dates, refresh_due dates, source_type, confidence, claim coverage, and caveats
first-party practitioner evidence must not be described as controlled research

sources.title: How to Run a Gauntlet Loop
sources.publisher: Something Big Is Happening, Matt Shumer
claims: The named method uses a lead agent, a concrete inspectable bar, decomposed pieces, separate fresh-context critics, direct inspection of the artifact, and repeated refinement.
The author explicitly says the game did not become better than Call of Duty and that the human stopped the run.
The author describes one initiating prompt followed by many hours and many subagents, not one model completion.
The author recommends a whole-artifact smoothing pass after waves of separate changes.
caveats: This is the method author's own explanatory and promotional account, not a controlled comparison.
Its generalization claims are hypotheses until tested per domain.
Current product and model recommendations can drift quickly.

sources.title: Claude of Duty README and honest assessment
claims: The repository reports roughly 55,000 lines across 11 subsystems and describes its capture, baseline, image-diff, profiling, and playtest tools.
The stated goal was to match a modern Call of Duty, and the repository says it did not.
Critic scores were 3.59, 4.14, 4.05, and 5.05 out of 10, so progress was non-monotonic.
Every critic in every blind comparison round selected the real Call of Duty frame.
For coupled lighting concerns, three six-agent directory-owned rounds left defects at 60, 47, and 66, while a sequential single-owner pass cut defects from 66 to 26 and moved the score by 1.00.
caveats: The measurements and critic protocol are reported by the builder and were not independently audited for this source pack.
The process finding is strong project evidence, but one project does not establish a universal causal rule.
Repository content can change, so release integrations should pin a commit or capture a hash.

sources.title: Claude of Duty original prompt
claims: The original prompt asks for a concrete Call of Duty comparison, subagent fan-out, a separate harsh visual critic, blind side-by-side comparison, and repeated looping.
The original prompt contains aspirational quality language but does not itself prove that the output met that quality bar.
caveats: A prompt is evidence of instructions, not evidence of resulting quality, cost, causality, or reproducibility.
The prompt should be read together with the repository's contrary honest assessment.

sources.title: Building effective agents
claims: Evaluator-optimizer workflows fit tasks with clear evaluation criteria and measurable value from iterative refinement.
Orchestrator-worker workflows dynamically decompose tasks and synthesize worker results.
Parallel sectioning is for independent subtasks, while agentic systems trade latency and cost for performance.
Ground truth from the environment and explicit stopping conditions help maintain control.
caveats: This is vendor guidance based on Anthropic experience, not a controlled Gauntlet Loop benchmark.
The page itself warns that much of the tooling landscape described in 2024 has changed.

sources.title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
claims: Long-running work needs explicit state artifacts and clean handoffs across context windows.
Compaction alone was insufficient in Anthropic's application-building experiments.
Attempting too much at once and later declaring incomplete work done were observed failure modes.
caveats: The experiments concern Anthropic's harness and application-development setup, not the Gauntlet prompt in isolation.
Model and harness behavior is fast moving.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
claims: Agent evaluation should distinguish transcripts from actual end-state outcomes.
Code-based, model-based, and human graders have different strengths and should be selected by task.
Model graders require calibration with human graders, and regression suites are needed to detect backsliding.
Multiple trials are needed because agent behavior varies between runs.
caveats: This is vendor guidance and includes illustrative examples, not a universal benchmark result.
Evaluation design must be adapted to the artifact and risk.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
claims: Anthropic found multi-agent research useful for breadth-first queries with independent directions.
Anthropic reports that multi-agent systems used about 15 times the tokens of chats in its data.
Anthropic says domains with shared context or many dependencies are not a good fit for current multi-agent systems.
Durable execution, retry logic, checkpoints, tracing, clear subagent boundaries, and explicit guardrails were important in production.
caveats: The 90.2 percent result is an internal vendor evaluation on a research task and does not establish gains for coupled code or creative work.
The token multiples describe Anthropic's system and should not be used as universal cost forecasts.

sources.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
claims: Across seven evaluated tasks, iterative same-model feedback and refinement improved average task performance by about 20 percentage points over one-step generation in the reported setup.
The study capped runs at four feedback-refine iterations and used task-specific stop conditions.
Specific, actionable feedback mattered, while external oracle feedback produced larger gains in one math setting.
Refinement could ignore feedback or introduce new problems, so improvement was not guaranteed per trial.
caveats: This study tests Self-Refine, not separate builder and critic agents or an open-ended Gauntlet Loop.
Results are task, model, prompt, and metric dependent and should not be generalized to current models without re-evaluation.

sources.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
sources.publisher: Shinn et al., arXiv and NeurIPS 2023
claims: Reflexion stores verbal reflections in episodic memory and uses them to guide later trials.
The paper reports improvements over baselines across sequential decision-making, coding, and language reasoning tasks.
Feedback can be external or internally simulated, but the quality and grounding of the signal affect what the memory teaches.
caveats: Reflexion is not a direct test of blind builder-critic separation or of the Gauntlet prompt.
Reported benchmark gains do not establish production reliability or unlimited-loop safety.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
claims: LLM judges can perform pairwise, single-answer, and reference-guided grading.
The study found position, verbosity, self-enhancement, and reasoning limitations in LLM judges.
Position swaps, stronger references, complete context, and human agreement checks can mitigate some judge errors.
No single benchmark determines model quality, so comprehensive evaluation is needed.
caveats: The study evaluates chat assistants and models available in 2023, not visual artifacts or current agent systems.
High aggregate agreement does not guarantee correctness on an individual judgment.

sources.title: SELF-[IN]CORRECT: LLMs Struggle with Discriminating Self-Generated Responses
sources.publisher: Jiang et al., arXiv and AAAI
claims: Across the studied models and tasks, models were not reliably better at discriminating among their generated alternatives than at generating initial responses.
Self-refinement cannot be assumed to improve results solely because the same model judges its own candidates.
caveats: This paper does not prove that a fresh instance or different model is automatically unbiased or correct.
The findings are scoped to the studied tasks, models, and evaluation framework.

sources.title: Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
claims: The study measured significant self-preference bias in GPT-4 under its experimental setup.
Lower-perplexity, more familiar text received higher LLM evaluations than human evaluations, even beyond literal self-generation.
caveats: Fresh context reduces builder-history contamination but does not by itself remove model-family or familiarity bias.
The study does not validate blind A/B as sufficient for trustworthy acceptance.

sources.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
claims: An agent can satisfy a literal objective while failing the intended outcome.
Proxy metrics, incomplete specifications, evaluator blind spots, simulator flaws, and reward-channel manipulation can all create gaming opportunities.
More capable optimization can make specification failures more consequential.
caveats: Most examples concern reinforcement learning, but the objective-misspecification mechanism is relevant by analogy to iterative agent graders.
The source does not prescribe a complete governance system for generative-agent loops.

sources.title: Our framework for developing safe and trustworthy agents
claims: Humans should retain control over how agent goals are pursued, especially before high-stakes decisions.
Anthropic describes read-only defaults, explicit approval for mutations, stop controls, transparency, and layered defenses as parts of trustworthy agent operation.
caveats: This is Anthropic's own policy and product framing, not an independent safety evaluation.
Exact permission behavior varies by product, configuration, and release.

sources.title: Towards a science of scaling agent systems: When and why agent systems work
claims: Google Research reports a controlled evaluation of 180 agent configurations across five architectures, three model families, and four benchmarks.

Centralized coordination improved the parallelizable Finance-Agent task by 80.9 percent over a single agent, while every tested multi-agent variant degraded sequential PlanCraft performance by 39 to 70 percent.
Independent multi-agent systems amplified errors by 17.2 times in the reported evaluation, compared with 4.4 times for centralized systems.
caveats: These are results from the reported tasks, models, and harnesses, not a guarantee for every agent workflow.
The official article summarizes a linked paper. Equal-budget advantage for this Gauntlet Brain remains unvalidated.
